analysis.one_liner: Shifts liability for engine damage from high-ethanol fuel to the U.S. government.
analysis.headline: Backed by three Texas Democrats, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, the Environmental Protection Agency was weighing whether to allow gasoline with more than 10% ethanol (E15), and there were open questions about whether those blends could damage engines, especially in older cars, boats, and lawn equipment. This bill would have made the United States government the sole legal target for lawsuits over such damage, taking fuel manufacturers, refiners, retailers, and engine makers off the hook. Claimants could still recover their actual losses, but from taxpayers rather than from the industry, with no punitive damages, and only in federal district court. The bill never got any action in committee and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, fuel and renewable fuel makers, refiners, blenders, retailers, and manufacturers of engines and products that use fuel would have been shielded from lawsuits over damage caused by ethanol blends above 10%. That protection would also have reduced the legal risk of expanding ethanol blending, which the ethanol industry sought.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fuel makers, refiners, and engine manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: Any liability claim against a 'qualified entity' (anyone who makes, sells, distributes, or uses fuel, or makes products that use it) for damages caused by ethanol blends above 10% would be treated as a claim against the United States, and the government would be the only possible defendant [S2] [S3].
The bill waives the government's sovereign immunity specifically for these claims, so claimants could actually sue the United States rather than the industry [S2] [S3].
Recoveries would be capped at actual damages, eliminating punitive damages, and federal district courts would have exclusive jurisdiction over the cases [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would bear the cost of any damages from higher ethanol blends, since the federal government would be the sole defendant. Consumers harmed by engine damage would keep the right to recover actual losses but would lose punitive damages, and the companies responsible would pay nothing.

drawbacks.text: The bill transfers the full cost of any engine damage caused by higher ethanol blends to taxpayers, so the companies that put the fuel into commerce would face no liability of their own [S2] [S3].
Capping damages at actual losses removes punitive damages, which are the part of liability law that most strongly deters companies from ignoring known risks [S2] [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledged that there was insufficient data on how higher ethanol blends affect older vehicles and nonroad engines, and that federal testing was still underway, yet it would have locked in the liability shift in advance of those results [S3].

A supporter would counter that the bill offered legal certainty that could speed approval of a domestic renewable fuel, and that routing claims through federal court against the government still guaranteed victims compensation for real losses [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine benefit to fuel and engine makers: certainty that a policy change the EPA was considering would not expose them to lawsuits. The cost fell on everyone else — taxpayers would pay the industry's potential damages, and consumers would lose punitive-damage recourse. Because the science on older vehicles and equipment was unresolved when it was drafted, the public would have absorbed a risk the bill's own findings called uncertain. On balance, the protection ran to industry and the bill ran against the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on September 29, 2010, and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles A. Gonzalez of Texas introduced the bill on September 29, 2010, with Reps. Gene Green and Ciro Rodriguez as original cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, the only action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much: fuel and engine makers never got their liability shield, and taxpayers were spared being made the sole payer for any engine damage from higher ethanol blends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, spared the industry's liability bill

for.name: Rep. Charles A. Gonzalez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill shifting ethanol-blend liability to the federal government.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (Chair John Conyers)
against.role: Chair of the House Judiciary Committee, 111th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Texas Democrats supported the bill and no vote was ever held, so no partisan split ever showed up in the record.

industries.industry: Fuel refiners, blenders, and ethanol producers
industries.note: The bill would have shielded anyone selling or distributing fuel from lawsuits over engine damage caused by blends above 10%, making taxpayers the sole payer instead. Their gain comes directly at the public's cost.

Makers of any product that uses fuel would have been shielded from ethanol-damage claims, including for older cars, boats, and outdoor equipment. Consumers would still recover actual damages, but from the government rather than from the responsible companies.
Retailers, who feared customer lawsuits if higher blends damaged vehicles, would have been relieved of that risk at taxpayer expense.
